statement: A team of 3 is chosen from 4 girls and 3 boys. The team must include at least one boy. How many different teams are possible?

choices.misconception: I counted the teams with no boys, which are the ones that are not allowed.
I counted only the teams with exactly one boy and forgot teams with two or three boys.
I counted every team of 3 and forgot the rule about including a boy.
I chose one boy first and then any 2 of the other 6, so teams with two or three boys got counted more than once.

hints: Is it easier to count the teams that break the rule?
Count all teams of 3 from the 7 people, then take away the teams that have no boys. This avoids splitting into cases by the number of boys.
There are 35 teams of 3 from 7 people. Teams with no boys come from the 4 girls only, and there are 4 of those.

solutions.reliable: Split by the number of boys. One boy: 3 choices of boy and 6 pairs of girls, so 18 teams. Two boys: 3 pairs of boys and 4 choices of girl, so 12 teams. Three boys: 1 team. Total 18 + 12 + 1 = 31. The transferable idea: when choosing a group with a condition, split into cases that do not overlap and add them.
solutions.elegant: Count the opposite. There are 35 teams of 3 from 7 people (7 x 6 x 5 / 6). Teams with no boy come only from the 4 girls, and there are 4 of them (leave one girl out). So 35 - 4 = 31 teams include a boy.

whyOnTest: "At least one" signals counting the opposite, and choosing one boy first is the classic overcount.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
